speechtext: Go ahead.

subtopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
I would also ask that old age
pensioners be allowed to receive $500 a year, instead of the $365 they are allowed at the present time, without having their pension cut down. We should adjust soldier settlers' debts in accordance with the proposal I made when I spoke here on February 3. A resolution to that effect is now on the order paper. And for the boys and girls fighting the present war we should give them a square deal right from the start, not twenty years after they come back, but immediately they come back. I believe my colleague the hon. member for Camrose (Mr. Marshall) has on the order paper a resolution dealing with that.
The question is bound to come up, where ' will you find the money? I would ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) to tell us where he is finding the money at the present time for the war. If he is unable to get an answer to the question among his officials and advisers, I would like him to come across to the left centre group pointed out by the hon. member for York-Sunbury and we can tell him how to get it.

subtopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
I hesitate to
follow the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) in his remarks any further than the last he made in connection with old age pensions. I would suggest to him that if he or any of his friends wants an old age pension, provision already is made. Since 1908 we have had

Post-War Reconstruction
government annuities under which by contributing to them at any time after five years of age one can have any kind of old age pension he wants. There is nothing to prevent anyone from having an old age pension even at twenty-one years of age if he pays for it.
In its approach to this important question of reconstruction I am satisfied that this parliament has before it one of the most difficult tasks that has ever faced any parliament, namely, to devise some programme whereby it can create a condition of affairs to carry us successfully through the post-war period. I rather take the view of the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) and also of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that the winning of the war is the primary object. Whatever we do in the future will be more or less dependent on how this war is won and on the terms of the peace. No country to-day can live to itself; it will be dependent on the economic and other conditions that exist in other countries, because we shall have to dovetail our own economic life in a measure into their desires. Another thing that we should keep in mind is that while we are anxious to raise our standard of living we must not allow it to rise in excess of those of other countries because, if our standard of living is much higher than theirs it will be difficult for us to secure world trade and a proper world balance, inasmuch as we shall not be able to compete with them. That must be kept in mind. I know there are those who take the view that "as long as I get what I want I do not need to worry about the other fellow." But that philosophy is wrong; it cannot exist in this time; it could only lead to a repetition of the same disaster again. Furthermore, I say, as the Prime Minister said, that if the new order is not here and now we shall never have a new order.
I am prepared to say that the conduct of this war by this administration is making a great contribution to the post-war period in Canada. The conduct of this war, wise or otherwise, will leave an aftermath of difficulty and debt and disaster which, if not foreseen and avoided, will have to be paid for in the post-war period when the boys are returning. I would say that the wisdom of this government in introducing foreign exchange control, the excess profits tax and the regimenting more or less of industry in regard to price control, has had a great influence in maintaining an economy that will keep things on an even keel so that we shall not create loans which will only create disaster and depression afterwards. I believe that the contribution which this government is making will be very helpful in the post-war reconstruction period.
Unfortunately a great deal of pressure is being brought to bear by labour and even by our farmers to break this control system. While we do have to suffer some disabilities in consequence of control we should bear in mind that as consumers we enjoy the benefit of the holding down of our cost of living, and to that extent we should at least be fair enough to bring that side of the question to the attention of the public.
I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) last evening, in the course of which he stated that the depression of 1930 was caused by the selfishness of the great financial interests. I should like to approach that question from another point of view. I believe the depression of 1930 was caused more by the unusual prosperity that was enjoyed by a certain group of mediocre-minded people who had saved some money and who wanted to copy some of the richer people. They went into the stock market and took away control of many industries by bidding more for the stock than its earning power justified. As a result, a good deal of our industry got into the hands of men who did not know how to run it. They may have been good labour men but they were not capable of administering industry. Therefore I warn the committee, the house and the country that we must not permit any situation to exist under which people will administer affairs which they are not capable of administering. It seems to me that if we develop a nationalized industry there will be great danger of another depression, because the same element of society might obtain control of any government which would have the responsibility of nationalizing industry, and this would lead only to a repetition of the depression of 1930.
The hon. member for Vancouver East also had something to say about the accomplishments of our great ally Russia. I should like to direct attention to the fact that a great deal of the success Russia has achieved has been as a result of the help of the capitalistic, democratic countries, and that Russia is enjoying her present position because the capitalistic countries shared the knowledge and improvements that had been brought about under the system of free enterprise.
In these days we are subjected to many catch-phrases designed to have people believe that on account of the mercenary motives of some people, many in this country do not receive their fair share of the national income. It has been said that in 1942 we produced $9,000,000,000 worth of goods, of which we
Post-War Reconstruction

have marketed about $7,500,000,000 worth. Who got that money? Well, labour got over $4,000,000,000; the farmers got over $1,000,000,000, and those who had their money invested in industry got only $318,000,000. To those who believe that labour is not getting its share I ask, if you took the $318,000,000 and added it to the $4,000,000,000, do you think that would satisfy labour? I yield to no man in my desire to serve labour, but I know that the sober-minded labour man realizes that he must have industry as a place where he can sell his labour, and that he would not be doing labour any kindness by draining off all the profits so that there would be nothing left to plough back into more factories and equipment to create more employment. I only hope and trust that this reconstruction committee will keep some of these fundamentals in mind, and not be carried away by those catch-phrases which are intended only to divert the attention of the people from the really important matters in order that those who wish to fool the people [DOT] may gratify their own desires.
Then I hope the committee will give some consideration to our agricultural problems. In spite of all that has been said about farming I believe that, after all, the farm is a fairly good place to settle a large part of the population of Canada. In spite of all its disadvantages; in spite of all the hard work involved, I believe the farm offers a security that can be found nowhere else. If a man owns a farm he has a security which it would cost another man thousands of dollars of invested capital to obtain. If I may be allowed a personal word, the other day I sat down at my table on my own farm and enjoyed a meal cooked by my good wife. The only things on that table that were not grown on my farm were the pepper, salt, sugar and tea. Everything else was produced on my own land.

speechtext: And grown well.

subtopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
It was certainly well cooked. Where else could a man get security to compare with that? I have reached the point where I deplore the practice of some who call themselves dirt farmers but who seem to talk about only the unfavourable aspects of farming. They have more or less discouraged our youth from wanting to go on the land, and now they wonder why they are short of help. If agriculture is to have its proper place in the national life of Canada we must give it some self-respect. I have no intention of shutting my eyes to its weaknesses, but at least I can be honest enough to give it the credit it deserves.
